extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and informed readers of U.S. constitutional and governmental institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and normative criteria for how the U.S. Senate, the Presidency, and related institutions (nominations, treaties, civil service) ought to function and be selected; discusses consultation, selection, training, and institutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine consultation requires equality of voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument and an unobstructed interchange of views upon a ground of absolute equality are essential parts of the substance of genuine consultation between the President and the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The President, in practice, has no voice in Senate conclusions about diplomatic transactions; written messages and the offices of friendly Senators are inadequate substitutes. Executive sessions that exclude the President prevent real consultation. Genuine consultation implies face-to-face meeting and equal debate, not mere submission for endorsement or condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee-only consultation is inadequate for executive matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The committee machinery (e.g., Standing Committee on Foreign Relations) is the Senate's practical channel for consulting the President, but it is far less than a voice in the Senate's deliberations and is almost like dealing with a foreign power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary of State or other executives may confer with committee chairs, yet this predisposes the Senate to an attitude different from free, equal consultation with the President. Reliance on committees should not substitute for direct, equal engagement when genuine consultation is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominations should reflect merit, not patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominations ought to represent honest, demonstrated worth rather than the personal preference of the President or the intrigues of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like Smythe (1869) show how patronage and lobbying can block appointments and halt Senate business. Civil service reform is praised as a remedy that will make nominations based on merit and reduce factional blocking and scandalous transactions that attract public attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid private practices that give individual Senators undue weight
rubrics_metrics.description: The privacy of 'executive session' and understandings that a Senator's wishes for his State outweigh broader considerations allow irresponsible dictation and manipulation of appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privacy shields such practices from public condemnation; the President often hears only final votes and is excluded from the process. Transparency and procedures that prevent a single Senator from having disproportionate veto power are implied remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature should be able to coordinate confidentially with executors where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unfortunate that Congress governs without being put into confidential relations with the agents through whom it governs; dictation to a coordinate executive branch without cooperative channels is problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter argues for more effective channels of confidential and cooperative management between Congress and the executive, rather than remote dictation through votes and public decrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offices and roles should have coherent, functional design (Vice-President example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vice-President's office is anomalous and of insignificant, uncertain place in the constitutional framework; offices should have clear, defensible functions and stature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Vice-President is neither properly legislative nor executive and only gains stature via succession; institutional design ought to avoid such ambiguous, functionless offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional change should respect formal amendment processes where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Resorting to extra-constitutional fictions to adapt the Constitution indicates that the legal amendment machinery (Article Five) is too slow, but such informal change has significant political consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While practical needs have led to informal adaptations (e.g., party conventions supplanting intended elector functions), the author highlights the tension and implies preference for more principled, accountable processes rather than ad hoc fictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential selection should not be dominated by party-controlled electors
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitutional ideal of independent electors has been supplanted by party conventions and caucuses that effectively control electors; this undermines the original design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical evolution from free electors to partisan conventions and national party machinery is criticized as substituting an ideal non-partisan choice with a party-whipped process. The criterion favors selection mechanisms that better reflect independent judgment rather than party control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for executive candidates with administrative experience (governors over legislators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Congress is not a school for administrators, it is more rational to choose Presidents from executive experience (e.g., state governors) than from legislative eminence alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative distinction: Congress trains law-makers, not administrators; governors' responsibilities resemble the Presidency and thus provide better training. The chapter notes the trend toward choosing governors and argues that such experience better fits presidential duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection processes should favor leaders who have been publicly tested in management and leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary systems select leaders by long, open trial in debate and business management; our convention system does not provide the same continuous, public testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commons' method of self-selection by demonstrated leadership in debate is contrasted with the U.S. convention/nominating system. The implication is that selection methods which enable prolonged public testing of capacity for leadership are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential effectiveness depends on training and continuity, not necessarily short terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration must be learned by apprenticeship; short terms which cut off the efficient as well as the inefficient are repugnant to effective government. Efficiency should be the foundation for confidence in a public officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments against rigid short terms: Presidents are often dismissed soon after learning duties; a career path and longer service can improve administrative competence. The text endorses building training routes (e.g., governorships) and questions reverence for short terms purely on republican principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalize administration via civil service and training schools for executives
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a need for proper schools and career paths (civil service, state executive offices) to train federal administrators and prepare men for the Presidency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals include a carefully graded, impartially regulated civil service permitting merit promotions up to high office and recognizing state governorships and other subordinate offices as constructive training grounds for federal administrative leadership. The text references proposals (e.g., Albert Stickney) for professionalizing aspects of the executive.
